nameStory: The 'spinosus' in this harvestman's scientific name means 'spiny' in Latin, referring to the small spines and projections found on its body and legs. Like all harvestmen, it gets its common name from the old folk belief that these long-legged creatures could predict weather and help farmers know when to harvest their crops.
description: The Spiny Harvestman is a delicate-looking arachnid with an oval body and extremely long, thin legs that can span several times its body width. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused together into what looks like a single oval piece, typically brown or grayish in color. These creatures are quite small, with bodies usually measuring just a few millimeters across, though their gangly legs make them appear much larger. They're part of the harvestman family, which are often mistaken for spiders but are actually more closely related to mites and ticks.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Single oval body segment that feels firm but delicate to the touch, unlike spiders which have a clear waist between two body parts

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Extremely long, thin legs that are fragile and may break off easily when handled - they feel wispy and thread-like

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Small spines or bumps on the body and legs that you can feel if you gently run your finger along them - gives a slightly rough texture

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny oval body just a few millimeters across, about the size of a small peppercorn, but leg span can reach across a quarter

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic bobbing motion and often freezes when disturbed, unlike the quick darting movements of spiders

habitat: Look for Spiny Harvestmen in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests and woodlands, particularly under logs, leaf litter, and loose bark. They prefer areas with rich, decomposing organic matter where they can hunt for small insects and organic debris. You might also find them in gardens and parks, especially near compost piles or areas with thick mulch.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and rocks. Look for them starting to appear in late spring as they begin their search for food.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily spotted moving about in the evening hours. This is also their main mating season, so you might see them gathered in small groups.
seasonality.fall: Still active through early fall, but beginning to seek out protected overwintering sites. They may be found clustering under bark or in rock crevices preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden away under logs, rocks, or deep in leaf litter. Rarely seen during cold months unless you disturb their hiding places on warmer winter days.

funFact: When a harvestman loses one of its long legs to a predator, the detached leg can continue to twitch and move for several minutes, acting as a distraction while the harvestman escapes - but unlike some lizards, the leg never grows back!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for daddy longlegs spiders, but harvestmen have a single body segment while spiders have two distinct parts separated by a narrow waist. Remember: harvestmen look like they're wearing a tiny backpack, spiders look like they have a belt cinched tight around their middle.
contextualKnowledge: There's often confusion about the name 'daddy longlegs' - it can refer to harvestmen like this species, cellar spiders, or even crane flies (which aren't arachnids at all). True harvestmen like the Spiny Harvestman don't produce silk or venom, making them completely harmless to humans.
compareHints: The Spiny Harvestman differs from its relative the Painted Harvestman mainly in the texture and spination of its body - you can feel the small spines when you gently touch it, while the Painted Harvestman tends to be smoother. Both are quite rare in New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings, so any harvestman with noticeable spines is worth photographing and reporting to local naturalist groups.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Painted Harvestman can be distinguished from its close relative, the Spiny Harvestman (Odiellus spinosus), by its decorative color patterns rather than prominent spines or projections on the body.
